Patrick, Joyancee, Chris, and Ayessa: Young lives snuffed out by extremism. ENDEAVOR Last Tuesday, Patrick Dylan Wee, 15, was shot dead in his Grade 10 classroom at Ateneo de Zamboanga on Tuesday morning, August 18 by a fellow student named Mohammad Mael Jalani. The shooter subsequently died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.. This woeful incident happened barely a month after three students were killed in a similar shooting spree at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City. They were Joyancee Separa, Chris Lorenz Fabian, and Ayessa Nicole Dazo. Their “final moments reflected courage and resilience amid the chaos,” according to accounts from witnesses. Patrick’s intelligence, dedication, and passion for learning made him an exceptional young achiever who inspired many. In 2024, Patrick received a Gold Award at the International Mathematics Olympiad of Southeast Asia (IMOCSEA), representing the Philippines and bringing pride to his school and country. There is a growing wave of public outcry for more effective deterrents that would shield young students from the danger that lurks in their campuses and classrooms. Former Rep. Ashley Acedillo and cybercrime warfare expert Angel Redoble weighed in on what must be done when interviewed in Christian Esguerra’s podcast. Clearly, this complex problem calls for a concerted response from key stakeholders, including parents-teachers associations (PTAs), law enforcers, legislators and civil society advocates. The phrase “nihilistic violent extremism” (NVX) has emerged as a catch-all concept that invites deeper analysis, understanding and resolve to neutralize the malefactors that have led to the spread of this social malady. Recalling my early schooling, those were years of blissful maturity from boyhood to adolescence. There may have been incidents of juvenile rivalry and after-class brawls, but these could be fairly characterized as high-adrenalin episodes that are definitely less severe from the deeds that have spurred widespread concern and condemnation. Ironically, the Ateneo de Zamboanga community even held a drill simulating a similar emergency situation about a month ago. This would have prepared the teachers, students, and employees to respond in a more orderly manner to what transpired last Tuesday. But no simulation could have been totally predictive of what actually transpired. Still, there were red flags that manifested themselves earlier that should be analyzed systematically, Rep. Acedillo points out. Students’ propensity for video games should be redirected and channeled toward safe options. This is what new laws enacted in the United Kingdom seek to achieve. Mr. Redoble bats for cutting off communication lines between radical elements and those sections of the studentry that are still largely unaffected by the malady. Interviewed by Christian Esguerra, Regina Cabato who served recently Manila reporter for the Washington Post, emphasized the importance of assembling first all the relevant facts before unleashing speculation on what really happened and why. She said that parents must assume primary responsibility for monitoring what type of information is being consumed by their children. She says that a lack of vigilance could trigger the onset of a contagion effect that would make it extremely difficult for school authorities to act in a timely manner. She observed that historically, shooters have been motivated by the high attention they receive, She notes, “Hindi dapat silang i-like nang basta-basta lang.” Parents, school authorities, and other monitors should watch out and prevent the spread of content that is “dehumanizing” and “traumatizing.” She also bewailed the type of coverage in both traditional and social media, that seemed to focus on a “single cause” even if facts are insufficient and to deliver “blow by blow” narratives that unduly whet the public’s appetite for sensationalized reports. Ms. Cabato also noted that in their media statements, the government authorities exhibited a propensity to offer theories that lacked factual support. In the future, drills should be more generic in approach, according to Ms. Cabato. These should seek to raise consciousness on emergency preparedness to ensure a measured response that is not characterized by panic nor excitement. For its part, the Psychological Association of the Philippines (PAP) proposed the formulation of guidelines on reporting that respects privacy, avoids “glorification”, and focuses on post-incident recovery. One vital lesson has emerged: Attention-seeking attackers seem to have a fixation for self-glorification. In the end, let not this all-important lesson be lost or forgotten: “It is heartbreaking that a life filled with so much promise was cut short inside a classroom — a place meant for learning, growth, and safety.”. It is our shared responsibility to prevent its recurrence. Comments may be sent to sonnycoloma@gmail.com

Sustainability in retail and hospitality. HEARD IT THROUGH THE GRIPE-VINE While it is encouraging to note that the concepts of Sustainability and ESG (Environment, Social & Governance) agendas have progressively entered the mainstream, and enjoy extensive media coverage; the fact remains that for many, it’s about approval and agreeing with the concepts, but still not seeing them as courses of personal attention and/or individual action. The Manila Bulletin Sustainability forum we’ve been mounting since 2022 has been showcasing how progressive companies can embed Sustainability-driven initiatives in their corporate DNA; and the thrust has been to encourage our audience to adapt Sustainability, even if only on a soft impact basis, into their everyday lifestyles. Today, I’d like to highlight and commend a retail SME, and a hospitality resort; for embracing sustainability, and making it a cornerstone of why they exist, and how they operate. KOKO SLOW Living - In the course of my dealings through the years with SM investments corporation, I’ve been lucky to meet people I like to consider are friends as well. Koleen Davila-Palaganas, VP and head, SM group Sustainability office at SM investments corporation, is one such person. So I’m proud to be able to say that I was around when she embarked on a personal passion project in 2024 - her small batch, handmade natural products for home and personal care. The SLOW stands for Sustainable, Local, Organic and Whole, the four cornerstones of the brand’s value proposition; and how it aims to make sustainable living accessible for every Filipino home. The first line of products were hand-poured soy candles in acacia wooden bowls that were sourced from carvers in the Mountain Province, and nourishing facial and body soaps that I admired for their natural ingredients and fine quality. The candles would be topped with dried flowers and herbs - a really great touch. While the soaps would come in unique shapes, and really highlight the core ingredients. Kultura is Koleen’s major retail partner, and they’re now located in 8 sites; and she has expanded the brand to Shopee and Lazada. They’ve since developed plant-based, non-chemical home care products that include laundry soap, fabric softener, and dishwashing soap. They have a wonderful linen spray, and now offer plant-based pet care products - a shampoo and conditioner, a pet balm, and a fresh breath oral spray. KOKO SLOW Living has new packaging, and when I mentioned to Koleen that I would write about it, she insisted that I credit Kultura, as they’ve been such a supportive retail partner from the very beginning. The people at Kultura were the ones guiding her on this repackaging, and I love the new, improved packaging. If KOKO is about elevating the everyday rituals of personal and home care into moments of calm, care and intention; the evolution of the products and the packaging are so in harmony with this vision. It’s a constant balance for Koleen, her position and duties with SM investments on one hand, and her role as entrepreneur/founder of KOKO SLOW Living. So I can only salute the great work she’s accomplishing on both fronts; and wish her the best. Anya Resort Tagaytay is situated at Buenavista Hills, technically falling under Silang, Cavite, but of close proximity to the Tagaytay ridge area. It’s led by Anya Hospitality Corporation and Roxaco Land Corporation, and gained formal acceptance into the Small Luxury Hotels of the World shortly after its’ 2017 opening. Just recently, Anya was included in this year’s Michelin Guide Selection of Hotels in the Philippines. And I was happy to be invited to their ninth anniversary celebration. Themed Reflections, I enjoyed the collaboration between Chef Chele Gonzalez of Samira and guest Chef James Antolin of Ikomai Tachi. It resulted in a reimagining of Spanish and Japanese street food, delectable roasts, and a bounty of desserts - via the terrific buffet spread. But what really struck me was when both Anya GM Mikel Arriet and Resort Manager Melody Amacio reiterated their commitment to responsible and sustainable hospitality. It’s about conscious luxury, and curating meaningful travel experiences; while recognizing how Sustainability is an increasingly defining factor for the discerning traveler of today. Anya is very proud of its Soulfully Sustainable program. It consists of multiple sustainable touch points - efforts in environmental stewardship, in community engagement, in cultural preservation, and in responsive tourism. The concrete measures taken to support this program have been recognized and lauded, both here and overseas. And this all falls under the belief ‘umbrella’ that exceptional and responsible hospitality should be creating a positive impact for the guests, for the staff, for the environment, and the local communities that the resort interacts with. Adapting Sustainability into one’s personal lifestyle is essentially about choices. And I’m happy to report how in diverse arenas such as Retail and Hospitality, there are players who recognize and adhere to the Sustainability imperative. If not now, when? And so now, it’s our move.

'One Night Only': Looking for love on the wildest night of the year. "One Night Only" is set in a strange present-day America where single people are forbidden from having sex for 364 days of the year. Then, for one night only, everything is allowed. People are in the streets, parks, subways and balconies, all trying to make the most of the one night they have. Basically, the entire country has one thing on its mind. In the middle of all those pheromones is Owen, a hopeless romantic who begins the night believing he has already found the person he wants to spend his life with. Instead, he gets dumped. Then there’s Allie, who is still looking for her prince, convinced that the right person is somewhere out there. What follows is a comedy of errors, with one misadventure after another bringing Owen and Allie together, separating them, then somehow putting them in each other’s paths again. Watching "One Night Only" felt like reading a really good rom-com novel. There are plenty of laughs, but they aren’t the usual slapstick kind. A lot of them come from surprise, awkward situations and just how ridiculous everything around these two people becomes. Considering the premise, though, the movie is surprisingly not sleazy. Yes, there are bodies everywhere. There are thongs. There are people getting it on practically anywhere they can find a spot. But you don’t end up focusing on any of that. The nudity and promiscuity are almost just part of the scenery. At its core, "One Night Only" is really a quest for love in the middle of a nationwide orgy. While everyone around them is desperately trying to find someone to sleep with before the night is over, Owen and Allie are looking for something more. The fun is watching two people who keep being pushed together while still looking everywhere else. For a movie with this much lust flying around, "One Night Only" is unexpectedly sweet. And by the end, it leaves you thinking about three very important things in life: love, lust and pizza. This is a great date movie, whether you’re single or you’ve been married for years and just want a fun night out together. It also feels different from the movies we’ve been getting over the past few months. The premise is wild, but it still gives you the things you want from a good romantic comedy: laughs, kilig, surprises and two people you want to root for. If you love rom-coms, this is one to watch. (Contributed by Margaret Rose Siytangco)

Marcos admin warns companies of EPR obligations. The Marcos administration is stepping up enforcement of the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Act as part of efforts to address plastic pollution and prevent garbage from clogging drainage and pumping facilities, Malacañang said. Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Undersecretary Claire Castro said this after President Marcos said garbage is one of the contributors to clogged pumping stations. In a press briefing, Castro said the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) is monitoring companies’ compliance with the EPR law by auditing their plastic waste recovery rates. “Aktibong binabantayan ng DENR ang pagsunod ng mga kumpanya sa EPR Law sa pamamagitan ng pag-audit sa kanilang recovery rates upang matiyak ang compliance (The DENR is actively monitoring companies’ compliance with the EPR Law by auditing their recovery rates to ensure compliance),” Castro said, quoting the DENR. The DENR has issued 155 show-cause letters to potentially obliged enterprises that may have failed to meet their EPR obligations. Republic Act No. 11898, or the EPR Act of 2022, requires large enterprises to recover and divert a portion of their plastic packaging waste through individual programs or collective organizations. The law amended the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 and sets increasing annual recovery targets for plastic packaging waste. For 2024, the mandated recovery target was 40 percent, while the audited recovery rates reached 59.98 percent for rigid plastics and 56.33 percent for flexible plastics. The recovery target will increase to 60 percent in 2026 and 80 percent in 2028. Castro urged the public to also do its part in properly managing and disposing of plastic waste, saying companies that comply with their obligations need the cooperation of communities. “So, kung ang kumpanya ay tumutupad sa kanilang mga alituntunin at kanilang obligasyon, makikiusap tayo sa ating mga kababayan, mga residente, na tumulong tayo (So, if companies are complying with their rules and obligations, we are asking our fellow Filipinos, our residents, to help us),” she said. Castro warned that companies that fail to recover their required plastic waste or otherwise violate the law could face multi-million-peso fines. “Sa mga kumpanyang hindi makaka-recover ng kanilang plastic waste footprint o hindi makakasunod sa mga requirement ng batas ay nahaharap sa mga multi-million-peso na multa (Companies that fail to recover their plastic waste footprint or comply with the requirements of the law face multi-million-peso fines),” she said.

A journey into Lagen Island Resort’s raw beauty, soulful craftsmanship, and quiet magic. There are places you leave behind, and there are places that stay with you. Lagen Island Resort–the enchanting reimagined island sanctuary in the heart of Bacuit Bay in El Nido, Palawan–belongs to the latter. There is something about the island that lingers long after you have left; mystical, enduring, intriguing, and very much alive. I found myself wanting to preserve every part of the experience through photographs, videos, anecdotes, and stories. But eventually, I realized that no image could quite capture what remained with me: the feeling. Lagen became a new core memory for me, and one of those rare luxury experiences that feels less like a stay and more like a passage into another world. Into the island The experience begins before you even set foot on the island. Whisked from El Nido town aboard a speedboat, with fresh fruits and refreshments served along the way, there is already a sense that you are leaving something behind and moving toward something different. As Lagen slowly comes into view, the anticipation builds. Our arrival at the Boathouse set the tone. Inspired by the “paraw,” the open-air structure feels warm and inviting, with earthy interiors and timber beams supporting a canted thatched roof shaped like the upturned hull of a sailing craft. It feels less like a reception area and more like the beginning of a story. “We really wanted Lagen to have its own personality, and it’s where connections blossom,” says Paloma Urquijo Zobel de Ayala, creative director of Ayala Land Hospitality. “It’s either you connect with nature, yourself, or family. What we’ve done is we’ve created a lot of experiences and spaces where that could happen.” That philosophy is evident throughout the resort’s refreshed design. Rather than imposing itself on the landscape, Lagen appears to have stepped back to allow the island to take center stage. “This allowed nature to come back and be the protagonist. Not the resort itself but the island,” Paloma explains. “You’ll see the Forest Rooms now have front and back views because we think that the limestone cliffs are as beautiful as the ocean views.” The approach is one of restraint, knowing what to remove rather than what to add. “It’s really about removing what isn’t necessary and practicing restraint. Even in the rooms, hopefully you have just what you need—the bare essentials for the modern-day traveler—without any unnecessary friction.” The renovation was completed in less than a year, while retaining as much of the existing footprint as possible. “Our goal was to cause the least amount of stress on the island, so we respected its existing footprint as much as possible. All the structures you see, except for the Wellness and Sports Center, were already there. We simply changed the materials and architectural language to give them a refreshed, contemporary identity,” Paloma says. Local culture is equally present, not simply as decoration but as a foundation for the resort’s new identity. “We really focus on three main crafts when designing the new refreshed and reimagined Lagen based on local Palawan culture, and those are pottery, weaving, and wood carving. You’ll see elements of those in different touch points around the resort.” Where nature leads Lagen is home to 42 thoughtfully reimagined Forest Rooms and Water Villas, set against an extraordinary landscape of dense forest, limestone cliffs, and clear waters. According to resort manager Andrew Fernandes, the vision was to create spaces and experiences deeply connected to Lagen’s natural surroundings while celebrating the Philippines’ rich cultural heritage. The accommodations are luxurious without feeling overly polished, drawing from Filipino traditions and indigenous art while working with contemporary artisans. Architectural nods to the traditional “bahay kubo” meet wall designs and partitions inspired by the Batak tribe’s Giyangganan weaving pattern. Throughout the interiors, motifs of the Tagbanua, Tausug, and Maranao people are subtly woven into the spaces, creating a visual language that feels distinctly Filipino without becoming literal. My Water Villa, one of 18 perched above the water, immediately felt like a retreat. Light pours into the space, creating a natural progression from the bedroom toward the veranda and, beyond it, the sea. A wooden door with etched detailing, coral marble bathroom surfaces, and handcrafted clay pieces bring warmth to the interiors. The “paraw” motif appears throughout—from etched patterns on sliding doors and ceilings to wave-inspired detailing on the veranda and the roof of The Clubhouse. Thoughtful touches include motion-activated night lights, bedside charging outlets, smart toilets, and double vanities. The closet comes stocked with stretch ropes, straw sun hats, slippers, and bags, and yoga equipment, while a Dyson hair dryer sits by the desk. On the veranda, a "sungka" set with shells quietly invites you to sit down and play. The Forest Suites, at 63 square meters, sit against the forest and limestone cliffs, with handcrafted woodwork and deep soaking tubs. Forest Rooms and Forest Deluxe Rooms offer more intimate retreats inspired by traditional weaving, ceramic bead patterns, and the surrounding landscape. Beyond architecture and interiors, Lagen’s spirit is expressed through partnerships with artisans across the archipelago. Artisano Kabalan of Olongapo brings its distinctive clay work, while Cavite-based Creaete Industrial Corp contributes intricate woodcraft rooted in Filipino, Spanish, and indigenous influences. Textile artists and weavers, including Wilson Limon of NiñoFranco, Jenny Mann, the T’boli Weavers, Gemma James Medel, and the Marabatuan Indigenous People Weavers Association, add layers of pattern, texture, and craftsmanship to Lagen’s contemporary interiors. At the table Dining is another important part of the Lagen experience, with El Nido Resorts executive chef Ric Ramos leading the culinary program. At The Clubhouse Restaurant, dining is accompanied by open views of the sea and resort, with seafood, local dishes, and international fare. The Boathouse transforms into a relaxed lounge beneath towering limestone cliffs, where handcrafted cocktails and light bites pair beautifully with the setting. And then there is sunset. From the Boathouse, the view opens dramatically toward the sea and sky, with the limestone landscape framing the horizon. Watching the light change across the water while sipping a drink was one of those moments that felt almost painterly—so beautiful that you instinctively stop talking. At The Beach Club, light bites and drinks come with views of the bay and Lagen Rock. For something more intimate, private dining can be arranged in caves, secluded coves, on sandbars, beaches, or a private deck. The island comes alive If nature is the protagonist, the experiences are what allow you to become part of the story. During my stay, I joined a sunset painting session by The Clubhouse, watched the 1957 classic “Badjao (The Sea Gypsies)” starring Rosa Rosal and Tony Santos Sr. near the caves, and took part in a weaving session with a local artisan. The weaving was particularly memorable for me. There was something wonderfully meditative about slowing down, learning the craft, and understanding the hands and traditions behind it. For the more adventurous, Lagen offers paddleboards, kayaks, eFoils, a Schiller bike, and Subnado sea gliders. On land, there are guided hikes to the majestic Lola Tree, island tours, and nighttime stargazing. Cultural experiences include the Kiminawit Village Tour, Pangangawil fishing, and visits to Kalye Artisano, where local craftsmanship takes center stage. Then there is the Lagen Wellness Sanctuary, with its tranquil garden, plunge pools, sauna, steam room, and treatment rooms. The Fitness Center provides strength equipment, free weights, and a yoga studio for those who prefer to stay active. But what I appreciated most was that there was never a sense that I had to do everything. Lagen allows you to move at your own pace. Sometimes the best experience is simply sitting still. Until we meet again Before leaving, we took part in one final ritual: crafting our own incense from local ingredients and offering blessings to the island. We placed our wishes and intentions into small bamboo boats and released them into the water with gratitude. Then it was time to say goodbye. As our boat pulled away, the Lagen team stood along the shore, waving enthusiastically until we were completely out of sight. It was a small gesture, but one I had never experienced quite like it before. Even in the goodbye, there was an unmistakable feeling that this was not really the end. At some point, it felt like you were already being invited to return. The waves grew bigger as we sped toward the port. Then, through the splashes of water, a rainbow appeared. It was perhaps the most poetic goodbye Lagen could have given me. And as the island slowly disappeared into the distance, I realized that perhaps this is the real luxury of Lagen. It is not simply the beautiful villa, the thoughtful design, or the food. It is the way the island stays with you. Some places you remember because of what you saw. Lagen, I believe, is remembered because of what you felt. How to get to Lagen Island Resort The journey to Lagen Island Resort begins with a flight to El Nido, Palawan. Guests can fly directly to Lio Airport from Clark, Bohol, or Cebu via private charter or Cebu Pacific’s commercial services, with flight times ranging from approximately 50 to 90 minutes. From Lio Airport, the journey continues by land and sea, with daily scheduled transfers taking guests to the resort. At the El Nido Resorts Jetty Lounge, travelers can take a breather and enjoy refreshments and local snacks before boarding the boat bound for Lagen Island.

A moderate earthquake shakes Japan, injuring more than 30 people in the Tokyo region. TOKYO (AP) — A moderate earthquake rattled eastern Japan, including the Tokyo area, early Sunday, injuring more than 30 people, most of them lightly, officials said. There was no danger of a tsunami. According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, the quake had a preliminary magnitude of 5.9 and its epicenter was in the southern Ibaraki prefecture with a depth of 70 kilometers (42 miles). The U.S. Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 5.8. At least 37 people were injured in five prefectures in the region — 15 in Tokyo, nine in Saitama, eight in Kanagawa, four in Chiba and one in Ibaraki — according to prefectural officials and the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. Most of the injured were hurt when they fell down or hit themselves against furniture or doors as they were caught off guard by the quake while sleeping and got out of bed in a panic, officials said. Among them was a woman in her 80s who fell off the bed and suffered a serious hip injury in Yokohama, in the Kanagawa prefecture, the Yomiuri newspaper reported. A 23-year-old man told the Asahi newspaper that he felt a vertical jolt seconds after his earthquake alert went off when he was shopping in Tokyo's eastern district of Taito. He said he feared getting hit by merchandise that fell from shelves as the building shook. The quake caused delays to express trains serving Tokyo and Narita Airport and other local trains serving northeastern regions, but Shinkansen bullet trains were running normally, their operator East Japan Raiway Co. said. The government set up a task force to assess the extent of possible damage, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on X. The Japan Meteorological Agency urged the residents in the area to use caution against another possible moderate earthquake for about a week. The temblor set off emergency quake alerts on mobile phones and also significantly shook Tokyo. NHK public television showed traffic on roads in nearby cities, including Mito and Saitama, seemingly normal. An underground water pipe ruptured in Tokyo's eastern ward of Koto, with water pouring onto the road, NHK footage showed. The pipe has been repaired and the leak stopped. There were no reports of anomalies from about a dozen nuclear power plants and other facilities that handle nuclear materials, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said. Last month, a magnitude 7.1 quake struck the Kumamoto area on Japan's southernmost island of Kyushu, killing 38 people and injuring 364.

Israel's deadly Gaza strikes cast doubt on ceasefire progress days after Kushner visit. DEIR AL-BALAH, Gaza Strip (AP) — Deadly airstrikes in Gaza on Wednesday cast more doubt on whether new U.S. efforts can advance a tenuous ceasefire in the Palestinian territory. Just two days after U.S. negotiators reportedly asked Israel to draw down attacks in the Gaza Strip, at least 10 people were killed Wednesday in two strikes, according to local hospitals and the Palestinian Red Crescent. Israeli troops also crossed the ceasefire line in southern Gaza and detained a Hamas police colonel at dawn Wednesday, two witnesses and a Hamas official said. Israel's military said one of the strikes on Wednesday, in the area of Nuseirat refugee camp, struck a Hamas commander who had participated in the Hamas-led attack in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in which 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were killed and 251 abducted. A second strike in the Tuffah area of Gaza City struck four Hamas militants gathering in a police station, the military said, claiming they were planning to carry out attacks against Israeli troops. Israel's military said a strike the day before targeted a meeting of four Hamas commanders and additional militants. The commanders killed included Muhammad Hamdi Ahmad Al-Masri, Muhammad Attar and Muhammad Fathi Hussein Nasser, all accused of carrying out terrorist attacks against Israeli troops, and Samed Samir Harb Abu Habal, who infiltrated Israeli territory during the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack, according to a statement from Israel's military. The Hamas-run Interior Ministry said the Wednesday Gaza City strike on the police station killed eight police officers and a 13-year-old girl. Two officers were women, it said. One person was killed in Nuseirat. On Tuesday evening, an Israeli strike on a busy seaside cafe killed seven Palestinians, including a child, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. Jared Kushner, a U.S. negotiator and President Donald Trump's son-in-law, held a marathon meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday, in which he asked Israel's leader to draw down attacks on Gaza, a person familiar with the meeting said. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief journalists. Also on Wednesday, Israel's military said it had completed reviews of 150 incidents of troop conduct during the war in Gaza and would launch criminal investigations into the 2024 killings of a 5-year-old girl and her family, as well as of 15 Palestinian paramedics in 2025. At least 17 killed in Israeli strikes The deadly strikes in Gaza on Tuesday and Wednesday exacted more casualties even as a ceasefire that's been in place since October has significantly diminished the fighting in the tiny enclave where more than 2 million Palestinians live. Since the ceasefire, Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,273 people, according to health officials in Gaza. The nearly three-year Israel-Hamas war has killed more than 73,400 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records viewed as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and international organizations. It doesn't distinguish between civilians and militants, but says women and children make up around half of the toll. In the early hours of Wednesday, at least 15 Israeli troops entered the Muwasi coastal area, west of the city of Khan Younis, two residents and a Hamas official said. Accompanied by armed men, the troops stormed the tent of Sabri Abdel-All, a colonel for the Hamas-led Blue Police in Khan Younis. They also detained another resident identified as Nashat Ezzat Zaarab, they said. The two residents and the Hamas official spoke on condition of anonymity for their safety. Latest ceasefire negotiations offer few concrete commitments On the diplomatic front, the ceasefire also appears stalled. Trump's initial ceasefire plan laid out a broad vision for ending Hamas' rule in Gaza and rebuilding the territory, much of which was reduced to rubble during the war. But since last fall, major sticking points have emerged on the conditions of Hamas' disarmament and Israel's withdrawal — and which should come first. Earlier this month, Trump announced that Hamas had agreed to disarm. But Hamas said it would begin to disarm if Israel halts strikes and withdraws, adding that laying down its heavy weapons would come later and be contingent on the creation of a Palestinian state — something Israel's government rejects. Netanyahu also pushed back on the deal, saying Israel won't withdraw from its current lines in Gaza until Hamas has completely disarmed. After Wednesday's strikes, Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem lashed out at the Board of Peace — the body Trump established to oversee the ceasefire — saying it has provided a "cover" for Israel to escalate its attacks in Gaza instead of pressuring it to abide by the ceasefire agreement.

What to know about Trump's 50% tariffs on Canadian goods that just went into effect. CHICAGO (AP) — After trade negotiations crumbled at the eleventh hour, U.S. President Donald Trump's 50% tariffs on scores of Canadian imports kicked in Saturday. The new levies are expected to affect about 5% of Canada's annual exports to the U.S., roughly $20 billion in goods ranging from hockey sticks to agricultural products. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney quickly promised Saturday that his government would roll out "dollar for dollar" retaliatory measures starting Sept. 8. No further talks are scheduled. The latest escalation between the two countries — which once held one of the world's most durable trade alliances — plunges them deeper into a trade war that has kept both sides of the border on edge throughout Trump's second term in office. Experts warn steeper tariffs raise costs for businesses and almost always trickle down to households in the form of higher prices. "Nearly all industries and professions are likely to see downstream effects from this spiraling trade dispute," said Augustine Lo, of law firm Dorsey & Whitney, whose work includes advising clients on international trade. Here's what we know. Which goods are affected? Again, the 50% tariffs from the U.S. are set to affect $20 billion of Canadian goods. Canada sends the vast majority of its goods exports to the U.S. (72% last year), and Trump administration says the new taxes will be levied on products ranging from hockey sticks to wine and cement. The list is long. According to documents published by the White House, other goods subject to the tax include honey, seeds and agricultural products — as well as select makeup, perfumes, clothing, jewelry, furniture, cameras, fabric and more. The 50% levy also applies to some products that were previously protected under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trade pact from Trump's first term. That marks a shift from past levies — and further underlines questions around the future of the USMCA overall. How is Trump imposing these tariffs? To impose these 50% tariffs, Trump reached back to a long-dormant Great Depression-era law: Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. When the U.S. and world economies were in collapse nearly a century ago, Congress passed the 1930 law as part of broader "Smoot-Hawley" legislation (named after its congressional sponsors). The act raised tariffs more generally across the board, and became notorious among economists for limiting world commerce and making the Great Depression worse. But Section 338 — which authorizes the president to slap import taxes of up to 50% on imports from countries that have discriminated against U.S. businesses — has never been used specifically to raise tariffs until now. No investigation is required to justify the levies. Nor is there any limit on how long they can stay in place. Since there's no precedent, however, the latest tariffs may also see more legal challenges. When announcing his planned tariffs last month, Trump claimed that Canada was unfairly discriminating against U.S. exports of automobiles, alcohol and dairy products. The president expressed anger over Canada's retaliation against his own tariffs last year — noting Canadian imports of American alcohol and cars started to fall last spring. Is Canada retaliating? Canada's Carney quickly promised to match the new levies "dollar for dollar" — later announcing retaliation would begin Sept. 8. He noted Canada's tariff increases would target steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics. The prime minister said Canada was willing to drop remaining retaliatory tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos if the U.S. substantially lowered its own, and to encourage provinces to restore U.S. alcohol sales. But eventually, he said Washington's final demands went too far. Carney accused Washington of using "economic integration as a weapon," and that Canada had been "attacked" by the latest U.S. tariffs. He said his country had the reserves and resilience to respond. Trump's top trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, pledged additional measures to respond to Canada's retaliation — without immediately specifying what that would look like. In a Saturday interview with "Fox & Friends Weekend," Greer also claimed the administration offered to cut tariffs on steel, autos and lumber, but Canada "didn't want" the deal. What's next? Tariffs are taxes paid by importers, or businesses that buy goods from abroad. That typically trickles down to consumers through higher prices — and, as seen over the last year, can also create uncertainty for workers across affected sectors. North America now has a "new tariff landscape," Dave Townsend, a partner at law firm Dorsey & Whitney, said Saturday. He noted a big question is whether the latest levies prove to be temporary. The 50% tariffs come on top of previously-imposed levies, including a 10% rate Trump slapped on Canada just last month ostensibly for failing to do enough to prevent imports produced by forced labor and separate sectoral levies impacting trading partners globally. The growing trade sanctions on Canada underscore Trump's willingness to risk breaking established alliances. And Canada's reluctance to accept a deal may reflect recent experience. Trump has repeatedly targeted Canada, even after instances where it made concessions following his demands. Some tolls on the newly opened Gordie Howe Bridge will be shared for 15 years, despite the fact that Canadians paid for the span linking Detroit and Windsor. Canada also withdrew a digital services tax last year. All the while, Trump has threatened more tariffs over everything from a TV ad criticizing his trade policies (later pulled by Ontario's government ) to wildfires that blackened skies across North America. Steeper tariffs have already contributed to higher inflation — but appeared to level off some in recent months, per researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, notably after the Supreme Court in February struck down some of Trump's most sweeping levies. Still, Saturday's taxes against Canada mark the latest instance of Trump turning to other laws to impose tariffs. And more recently, Washington's war with Iran has driven prices even higher. With the cost of living at the center of many voters' minds in a midterm election year, political ramifications could mount for the Republican president in the coming months.

73 families affected in Muntinlupa fire. Fire hit a residential area in Barangay Cupang, Muntinlupa, on Aug. 22, affecting 73 families or 194 individuals. The blaze started at about 10:17 a.m. in Bunyi Compound on East Service Road. Firefighters raised the first alarm at 10:25 a.m. before the fire was put under control at 11:13 a.m. and put out at 11:50 a.m. Muntinlupa Mayor Ruffy Biazon said the affected families are temporarily staying at Bunyi covered court. He ordered the city’s Social Services Department to provide assistance, especially essential non-food items like sleeping and hygiene kits, food packs and rice. The mayor assured families that they will be given financial support and referrals to other government agencies for special needs.

Iran security chief threatens neighbors against economic measures, and other Mideast developments. The new leader of Iran's top security body is threatening neighbors against joining new U.S. efforts to squeeze Tehran's economy. Egypt is trying to revive Iran-U.S. negotiations. And Iraq and Iran say Tehran has helped some ships carrying Iraqi oil to transit the Strait of Hormuz. France and Saudi Arabia are expected to discuss plans to bypass the waterway. Meanwhile, Israel has carried out strikes in Syria and in Gaza. Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Saturday. Full coverage can be found here. Iran's new top security adviser issues threats The hard-line new leader of Iran's Supreme National Security Council threatened Tehran's neighbors against joining the new U.S. effort to hurt Iran's economy, and accused the United States of increasing global nuclear insecurity with months of war. "If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner," he said in an interview with the state broadcaster that aired Saturday. Mohsen Rezaei was named this month as part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran's political and military stance. His interview with IRIB is his most extensive public statement since then. Rezaei said Iran would target oil-shipping routes out of the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz — if neighbors join what he described as the economic war against Iran. Those neighbors would be considered enemies and "we will target their interests," he said. U.S. President Donald Trump in the past week has vowed to increase Iran's pain by imposing an "unprecedented" level of economic warfare and isolation. Iran has lived under sanctions for years. Rezaei said discussions with Oman, located on the other side of the strait, over management of it were ongoing, and said fees would be imposed. Iran asserted control over what was seen as an international waterway shortly after the U.S. and Israel attacked on Feb. 28. Rezaei also vowed to make changes to Iran's diplomacy and bring new capabilities to what he called the next war. He warned the U.S. against sending more military personnel to the region, and said the U.S. had increased nuclear insecurity because countries see that participating in international monitoring efforts, as Iran has done, is no protection against attack. Egypt tries to revive US-Iran negotiations The top diplomats for Egypt and Iran discussed efforts to bring Tehran and Washington back to the negotiating table to settle the war, Egypt's foreign ministry said. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Egyptian counterpart Badr Abdelatty also discussed the Iranian-Omani talks, the ministry said. Araghchi briefed Egypt's foreign minister about "Iran's view of ongoing developments, the course of negotiations and their challenges," the ministry said, without elaborating. Araghchi confirmed the call. Separately, Araghchi said he had a call with Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, Iran and Iraq say some Iraqi oil is facilitated through the strait The governments of Iraq and Iran said Tehran has helped some ships carrying Iraqi oil to transit the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for global oil, natural gas and other supplies, but there were few details. "There is facilitation for some ships carrying Iraqi oil in the Strait of Hormuz," Iraqi President Nizar Amidi said in comments published Saturday by the state-run news agency, adding that Iraq doesn't have a national carrier for transporting oil. Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said a number of Iraqi oil tankers have been permitted to transit. It was not clear how many or what Iran might have received in return. Syria says an Israeli drone strikes inside a village An Israeli drone strike on a vehicle wounded one person on Saturday in the southwestern Syrian village of Beit Jin, according to the Syrian state news agency SANA. Syria's foreign ministry said several civilians were injured and called the strike a flagrant violation of the country's sovereignty. The Israeli military said it targeted a "terrorist who advanced terror attacks in final stages of preparation," without elaborating. It wasn't immediately clear if it was the same strike. Israel has carried out hundreds of airstrikes around Syria after the ouster of former President Bashar Assad in late 2024, mainly destroying army assets to keep them out of the hands of his successors. Messages differ on the Golan Heights In an interview on Friday with Mario Nawfal, a Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur, U.S. Ambassador Tom Barrack said Israel "still" occupies the Golan Heights in violation of U.N. resolutions. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Saturday in a statement called Barrack's remarks "full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict Trump's own position." Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 war and annexed it in 1981. The U.N. considers the territory occupied Syrian land. But in March 2019, Trump signed a proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, reversing decades of U.S. policy. French president and Saudi crown prince will meet French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman are expected to discuss plans to develop alternatives routes to the Strait of Hormuz during the Saudi leader's two-day visit to Paris that starts on Sunday, according to officials in the presidency who weren't authorized to be publicly named. Proposals include increasing trade through Omani ports outside of the Persian Gulf, expanding or doubling pipelines in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere, and developing new rail links, the officials said. France and Saudi Arabia have formed a task force on energy and logistics connections between the Middle East and Europe that is scheduled to meet at the ministerial level Monday. The officials said the work would focus on identifying the most strategic projects, securing financing and establishing roles for French companies. An Israeli strike in Gaza kills 1 Palestinian An Israeli strike on the backyard of a house in central Gaza killed one Palestinian and wounded another Saturday, according to health officials at Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital. Israel's military said it targeted Sharif al-Hasanat, a Hamas commander who "advanced terror attacks and took part in efforts to restore Hamas' underground infrastructure." Days earlier, a U.S. negotiator reportedly asked Israel to draw down attacks while seeking to make progress on the ceasefire.

When violent videos spread online, what should parents tell their children?. A few weeks ago, after several disturbing incidents involving young people, I wrote about children becoming desensitized to violence and how to reassure them when frightening news makes them ask, “Can that happen to me?” I did not expect to have both conversations with my own children this soon. The Aug. 18 shooting at the Ateneo de Zamboanga University Junior High School campus left two students dead, including the shooter, and two others injured. The incident was livestreamed, and authorities are investigating. For parents, difficult questions follow. How could this happen inside a school? How did a student get access to firearms? Could it happen where our own children study? There is another question we should ask—What are our children seeing on their phones right now? Talk to them before the internet does Conversations with our children can happen anytime and anywhere, during meals, in the car, while waiting for something, or when a child casually mentions something a classmate sent in a group chat. Sometimes they tell us something troubling almost in passing. We have to listen closely enough to notice. The relationship we have with our children matters. It does not mean they will tell us everything, especially as they get older. But if they know they can come to us without immediately being judged, lectured, or punished, there is a better chance they will talk when something is bothering them. There is no single age for these conversations. Even young children may hear about disturbing events from other people or media. What matters is keeping the explanation simple, honest, and appropriate for what they can understand. Start by asking what they already know, then answer their questions without giving graphic details. When I spoke with developmental pediatrician Dr. Jack Herrin about children becoming desensitized to violence, he stressed the importance of parents staying involved in what their children are exposed to and talking about what they see. When frightening news involves children their own age, we do not have to wait for them to bring it up. We can ask: Have you heard what happened? What have your friends been saying? Did anyone send you the video? Did you watch it? What was your immediate reaction? Psychologist Raph G. Doval-Santos gave similar advice when we discussed how children process frightening news. He suggested finding out how they feel about what they have heard or seen. Sometimes, a simple question such as “How does that news make you feel?” is enough to get them talking. Before starting the conversation, it also helps to make sure we are calm enough to listen. Whenever something like this happens, my husband and I usually talk about it first and remind each other, “We need to talk about this with the kids over dinner tonight.” We do not bring these things up to scare them. But staying silent does not mean our children will not hear about it from friends, group chats, or social media. We would rather talk about it with them and give them the chance to ask questions. That night, we stayed a little longer at the dining table and told our children what had happened. We also told them not to look for or watch the video of the shooting if someone sent it to them. We have had these conversations before, sometimes because of the things our children watch or the games they play. When our teenage son started playing first-person shooter video games, my husband would sometimes play with him and his friends. It became a way to bond, but also a chance to talk about the game and violence in general. Playing a shooting game was never the same as real-life violence in our home. We wanted our children to understand the difference between playing a game and what it means when someone is actually hurt or killed. We aren’t trying to interrogate them. We simply want to give them time to talk while we listen to what they really think or feel. We can also acknowledge that something frightening happened, answer what we can, and remind them of the people working to keep them safe. Our children should also know that if disturbing footage is sent to them or appears on their feed, they do not have to watch, respond, or pass it on. They can leave the group chat, block or report an account, and tell us what happened. If they have already seen it, try not to react with anger. Ask how it made them feel and give them time to talk about it. In the next few days, watch for trouble sleeping, unusual anxiety, or repeatedly returning to what they saw. Not everything needs to be shared The Zamboanga attack was livestreamed through a body-worn camera, giving viewers a first-person view of what happened. The footage itself is disturbing. As parents, it is even more worrying to know that our children could easily come across it online. We no longer have to search for violent footage to come across it. The same can happen to our children through their feeds, group chats, or messages from friends. The Council for the Welfare of Children has cautioned against circulating graphic clips and sensitive material involving minors following the shooting. The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center has also asked the public to stop spreading graphic images and videos connected to the incident. Manila Bulletin’s Information and Communications Technology Department assistant vice president, Art Samaniego Jr., made a similar appeal on his Facebook account: “Ang dapat nating gawing viral ay information on how to prevent another tragedy, hindi ang footage ng tragedy itself (What we should make viral is information on how to prevent another tragedy, not footage of the tragedy itself).” I couldn’t agree more. There is a difference between knowing what happened and watching it happen. We need the facts and answers about school safety and access to firearms. We do not need to keep replaying the moment someone was hurt or killed, or send it to our children. If footage may have value as evidence, it should be turned over to the proper authorities instead of posted publicly or forwarded to group chats. Parents also set an example. Before we forward something disturbing, we should ask ourselves: Does anyone really need to see this? If the answer is no, don’t share it. Stay close Talking about violence with our children should not begin only when something terrible happens. We can watch what they watch from time to time, ask about the games they play, know who their friends are, and listen when they tell us stories that may seem small. Our relationship with them is built on ordinary days, when we listen without turning every conversation into a lecture and make it clear that difficult subjects are allowed at home, even when the answers make us uncomfortable. There will be investigations into what happened in Zamboanga, and many questions will need answers. At home, we have our own work to do. When violent footage appears on our screens, we can choose not to pass it on. But just as important is making sure our children know they can come to us when something scares, confuses, or troubles them. We may not always have the answers, but we can be there to listen, talk, and help them make sense of what they see.

The CCP after EDSA I. The end of the Marcos administration in February 1986 ushered in a new political era—and a markedly different climate for the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP). With Imelda Marcos away, the CCP, and to some extent the arts, made way for other needs. The CCP, once a flagship institution, entered a period of institutional adjustment. The Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) called in the loans it had extended to finance CCP’s capital projects, leading to the foreclosure of the Philippine Plaza Hotel, the Coconut Palace, and the extensive parcel of land across Sotto Street from the CCP Main Building. President Corazon Aquino reportedly never set foot inside the CCP during her presidency. The institution also lost its exemption from civil service regulations, becoming subject to the procedures and constraints of an ordinary bureau. The country’s cultural landscape was also transformed with the establishment of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA). Organized on a more participatory model, with decision-making committees composed of artists and cultural practitioners, the NCCA assumed certain functions previously assigned to the CCP and received substantial public funding. A former CCP officer observed that artistic priorities shifted. It seems that productions tended to distance themselves from association with the Marcos years, turning instead to themes that examined Martial Law abuses and reflected more broadly on the failures of the Marcos years. To some extent, the arts became not only a vehicle for creative expression but also a means of historical reckoning. The late 1990s brought another period of turbulence as rival factions contested CCP’s leadership. Although the disputes were eventually resolved, they eroded staff morale and tarnished the institution's public standing. Tensions between the CCP and the NCCA also contributed to a prolonged impasse in the conferment of the National Artist awards, delaying the country's highest cultural honors for several years. As passions cooled, the CCP co-launched programs that have left a lasting mark. Virgin Labfest, launched in 2005, has become the country's premier showcase for new and untried theatrical works. Cinemalaya, established in 2005, revitalized independent Filipino filmmaking. These continue to be among the CCP’s most influential and popular activities. For much of its history, the CCP Board remained removed from the institution's day-to-day operations. I served briefly as a CCP Trustee in the early 1980s and recall attending only one board meeting. My impression at the time was that trustees were principally engaged in mobilizing financial support for the center's projects. I lost touch with the CCP over the next decades, but I am told that during those years, CCP functioned largely as a government bureaucracy, with authority concentrated in the president and senior management. Board meetings served primarily to update trustees on recent activities and secure formal approval for budgets, appointments, and other administrative matters. That was certainly the situation when I returned as a CCP Trustee in 2014.
